web.title: Modulating temperature and pH during subcritical water extraction tunes the molecular properties of apple pomace pectin as food gels and emulsifiers
web.description:
Apple pomace is composed of skin and flesh (95%), seeds (2-4%) and stems of apple (1%); with a content of pectin (3.5-14.3%), cellulose (13%), hemicelluloses (4.3%), starch (5.6%), fat (0.6-4.2%), protein (1.1-4.7%), polyphenols, vitamins and minerals (Lyu, et al., 2020;Perussello, Zhang, Marzocchella, & Tiwari, 2017). The main polyphenol groups present in apple pomace are phenolic acids (p-coumaric, caffeic, chlorogenic, protocatechuic), flavanols (epicatechin, procyanidin B2), dihydrochalcones and flavonols (hyperin, quercetin, avicularin) (Diñeiro García, Valles, & Picinelli Lobo, 2009;Schieber et al., 2003).

As another large constituent of apple pomace, pectin is a structurally heterogeneous polysaccharide typically composed of four domains with distinct branching patterns, namely homogalacturonan (HGA), rhamnogalacturonan-I (RG-I), rhamnogalacturonan-II (RG-II), and xylogalacturonan (XGA) (Fig. 1a). The main sugar constituent of the backbone of the different pectin domains is (1 → 4)-linked-α-D-galacturonic acid (GalA). HGA is defined as the smooth region of pectin, with acetyl and methyl esterification. XGA consists of an HGA backbone substituted by β-D-xylopyranose (Xyl), and methyl and acetyl esters. RG-I is a heteropolymer of alternating (1 → 2)-linked-α-L-rhamnopyranose (Rha) and (1 → 4)-linked-α-D-galacturonic acid units with substitutions of α-D-galactopyranose (D-Gal) and α-L-arabinofuranose (Ara). RG-II is known as the hairy region of pectin and contains the richest diversity of glycosidic linkages and sugars including L-Ara, L-Rha, D/L-Gal, D-glu- curonic acid (GlcA), apiose, aceric acid (3-C′-carboxy-5-deoxy-L-xylose), 2-O-methyl-L-fucose, 2-O-methyl-D-xylose, Kdo (3-deoxy-D-manno-2octulosonic acid) and Dha (3-deoxy-D-lyxo-2-heptulosaric acid). The smooth regions of pectin molecules can form a network via intermolecular bonds, resulting in gelation (Kastner, et al., 2014), depending on the degree of methylation (DM). The gelation of high methoxyl pectin (HMP) (DM>50%) is driven by hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds, and occurs in the presence of a co-solute (typically simple sugars) in acidic pH (≤3.5) (Tsoga, Richardson, & Morris, 2004). Low methoxyl pectin (LMP) (DM<50%), on the other hand, requires divalent cations (typically Ca 2+ ) for gelation, which forms intermolecular ionic junction zones between dissociated carboxyl groups. Due to this gelation capacity, pectin finds wide uses in the food industry as a gelling and thickening agent. LMP is particularly of interest as viscosifier to produce low-sugar products, specifically targeted for consumers with diabetes or obesity (Muñoz-Almagro, Montilla, & Villamiel, 2021). In the food industry, LMP is typically derived from HMP that is extracted from commercial pectin sources (e.g. citrus peel) (May, 1990). This requires the implementation of an additional processing step, increasing production costs. Direct extraction of LMP from plant tissues would, therefore, eliminate these additional steps. Conventional extraction of pectin is carried out using acid solutions and high temperature, despite its water-soluble characteristics. The use of relatively harsh conditions are required to disrupt supramolecular interactions between pectin and other plant cell wall components, which are known to be resistant to extraction (Sista Kameshwar & Qin, 2018). Subcritical water extraction (SWE) constitutes a promising technique for the extraction of matrix polysaccharides from recalcitrant plant cell wall tissues such as wood and grasses (P. O. Kilpeläinen et al., 2014;Ruthes et al., 2020). SWE uses water in liquid state at high pressure as a solvent, which undergoes physical changes such as lower viscosity and polarity, facilitating the extraction and diffusion of the target biomolecules (Plaza & Turner, 2015). In previous works, we have demonstrated that controlling the pH using specific buffers under SWE is an efficient tool to preserve the native functionalities (i.e acetylation and feruloylation) and to tune the physicochemical characteristics of polysaccharides from plant biomass using a single setup (Rudjito, Jiménez-Quero, Hamzaoui, Kohnen, & Vilaplana, 2020;Rudjito, Ruthes, Jiménez-Quero, & Vilaplana, 2019;Ruthes, Martínez-Abad, Tan, Bulone, & Vilaplana, 2017). In this work we hypothesized that the combination of acidic pH under subcritical water conditions would enable the extraction of pectins from apple pomace residues with a controlled range of DMs. We propose for the first time a cascade extraction process for the sequential recovery of polyphenols and pectin from apple pomace. We evaluated the antioxidant activity of the extracted polyphenols, and we monitored the time evolution of the pectin extraction at two different temperatures (120 • C and 140 • C) and 3 different pH conditions (pH 3.0, 5.0 and 7.0). The influence of the extraction conditions on the sugar composition, molar mass distribution, degree of methylation and rheological properties of the isolated pectins was also analyzed. Finally, as a proof of concept we evaluated the use of the apple pomace pectins extracted by SWE as vegetable oil emulsifiers together with their long-term stability.

Extraction of polyphenols The proposed cascade extraction of polyphenols and pectins from apple pomace is presented in Fig. 1b. For the extraction of polyphenols, apple pomace was milled in wet state using a kitchen blender and suspended in 50% (v/v) ethanol at 1:10 (pomace:solvent) ratio, following a procedure previously developed for sunflower hulls (Carolin Menzel, González-Martínez, Chiralt, & Vilaplana, 2019). The suspension was stirred for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Ethanol was evaporated using a rotary evaporator (Rotavapor R-210, Büchi Labortechnik AG, Switzerland) at 36 • C under vacuum in the dark and the concentrated phenolic extract was freeze-dried. 2.2.2. Extraction of pectins Subcritical water extraction (SWE) of polysaccharides from apple pomace was performed using an accelerated solvent extractor system (Dionex, ASE™ 350, Thermo Scientific™ Sunnyvale, CA, USA), following a similar approach previously developed for cereal bran (Ruthes, et al., 2017). The remaining apple pomace after the extraction of polyphenols was freeze-dried, weighed to 2 mg and then mixed with inert material in the extractor cells. Three cycles of sequential extractions were performed at pH 3.0, 5.0 and 7.0 for 5, 10 and 15 min at 120 • C and 140 • C. The extraction solvents were buffered with 0.1 M citrate buffer. The extracts were dialyzed using 3.5 kDa MWCO membranes for 72h and then freeze-dried. Extractions were performed in duplicate for each pH and temperature condition.

Total phenolic content Total phenolic content (TPC) of the extracted polyphenols was determined using the Folin-Ciocalteau assay. 100 mg/mL solutions of the samples were prepared in 50% ethanol and then filtered on filter paper. 100 μL aliquots of 10x dilutions of the solutions (10 mg/mL) were mixed with 100 μL of Folin-Ciocalteau reagent (2 N). After 2 min, 800 μL of sodium carbonate solution (20%, w/v) was added and the mixtures were incubated at 40 • C for 20 min in the dark. The absorbance was measured spectrophotometrically at 765 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Varian Cary 50 UV-VIS, Agilent) against water as blank. Gallic acid solution (0.01-0.08 mg/mL) was used as standard and the TPC of the extracted polyphenols was expressed in gallic acid miliequivalents (mg GAE)/g apple pomace.

Monosaccharide composition The monosaccharide composition of the apple pomace, SW extracts and residues was analyzed by high-performance anion-exchange chromatography with pulsed amperometric detection (HPAEC-PAD) after methanolysis and acid hydrolysis, respectively. On one hand, the apple pomace and hydrothermal (SWE) extracts were hydrolyzed in triplicate by 2-step methanolysis using 1-2 mg samples (Martínez-Abad, Giummarella, Lawoko, and Vilaplana (2018). Secondly, the apple pomace and residues after SWE were treated by 2-step sulfuric acid hydrolysis in triplicate (Saeman, Moore, Mitchell, & Millett, 1954). 3-4 mg sample was mixed with 72% sulfuric acid and incubated at room temperature for 1 h followed by dilution and hydrolysis at 100 • C for 3 h. The samples were then filtered with 0.45 μm nylon filters and diluted with ultrapure water (10x). The hydrolyzed samples were injected into the HPAEC-PAD system (Dionex ICS 3000, Sunnyvale, USA) equipped with a CarboPac PA1 column. Two gradient programs were used for the separation of neutral and uronic sugars, respectively (McKee, et al., 2016) and their quantification was performed by external standard calibration (0.005-0.1 g/L): fucose (Fuc), arabinose (Ara), rhamnose (Rha), galactose (Gal), glucose (Glc), xylose (Xyl), mannose (Man), galacturonic acid (GalA), glucuronic acid (GlcA) and 4-O-methyl glucuronic acid (meGlcA).

Emulsifying properties of the pectic fractions The emulsifying properties of two selected extracts from apple pomace with high and low methoxyl content were benchmarked with a commercially available high methoxyl citrus pectin control (DM of 71%) gently provided by Ceamsa (Porriño, PO, Spain) (Roman, et al., 2021).

Composition of the starting apple pomace As a by-product of apple processing, apple pomace was evaluated in this study as a rich source of phenolic acids and dietary fibre pectin to be valorized into antioxidant gels and emusifiers. The composition of the initial raw pomace was characterized in terms of moisture, protein and carbohydrate content (Table 1). The apple pomace contained 80.9% moisture as in agreement with previous studies (Fernandes, Ferreira, et al., 2019). Soluble proteins comprised a small portion (1.2%) of apple pomace and carbohydrates constituted its major components. As pectins, cellulose and hemicelluloses are the main polysaccharides of apple pomace (Perussello, et al., 2017), both sulfuric acid hydrolysis and two-step methanolysis were performed for the estimation of cellulose and pectin/hemicelluloses (neutral and uronic sugars), respectively. Sulfuric acid hydrolysis showed that fructose was the major monosaccharide in the apple pomace, followed by glucose. This glucose was attributed to cellulose, hemicellulose (e.g. xyloglucan and β-glucan) (Fernandes, Silva, et al., 2019) and starch (6.8%). Methanolysis, on the other hand, revealed the high abundance of pectic monosaccharides (GalA, Xyl, Fuc, Ara, Gal, Rha and GlcA), indicating the occurrence of different pectin regions (RG-I, RG-II, XGA and HGA). No fructose was detected after methanolysis, which was attributed to its complete degradation at hydrolysis conditions by furanoid dehydration (Becker, et al., 2021). 3.2. Characterization of extracted polyphenols The phenolic content and radical scavenging activity of the ethanolic extract were presented in Table 2. The ethanolic extract yielded a TPC of 8.2 mg GAE/g apple pomace, in agreement with previous studies where similar extraction methods were used (Ajila, Brar, Verma, Tyagi, & Valéro, 2011;Chandrasekar, Martín-González, Hirst, & Ballard, 2015). The content, as well as the profile of phenolics in apple pomace, varies depending on cultivar, the maturity of apple, growing and storage conditions and parts of apple that apple pomace was produced from (Diñeiro García, et al., 2009;Kalinowska, Bielawska, Lewandowska-Siwkiewicz, Priebe, & Lewandowski, 2014). The phenolic acid profile of the freshly extracted polyphenols, as analyzed by HPLC, showed a dominating content of chlorogenic acid (Supplementary Fig. S1) in agreement with previous studies (Diñeiro García, et al., 2009;Schieber et al., 2003). Five unknown compounds were observed between 32 and 37 min of the chromatogram (Supplementary Fig. S1), which may represent various phenolic families such as flavonols or dihydrochalcones (Diñeiro García, et al., 2009). However, these were not assigned to any phenolic compound as the UV-spectra did not correspond to the available standards. As for the radical scavenging activity of the extracted polyphenols, 19.4 mg extract was necessary to reduce 50% of 1 mg of DPPH • , suggesting a strong antioxidant activity that was attributed to the high phenolic content of the extract.

Time evolution of the monosaccharide composition during SWE The influence of process conditions (temperature, pH and time) on the monosaccharide composition of the extracted fractions under subcritical water was evaluated (Fig. 2c, Table 3). In general, all the extracts showed a predominant content of monosaccharides present in pectins such as GalA, Ara, Gal and Rha, indicating the selective extraction of pectic polysaccharides, mainly linear HG and RG-I. The low presence of Fuc and GlcA in all the extracts at different time and pH conditions may indicate that the presence of RG-II was limited. In parallel, the residues exhibited higher content in Glc, Xyl and Man, which indicates that cellulose and hemicelluloses (xylans and mannans) were enriched in the residue and not extracted at the tested SWE conditions.

As reported earlier, in the first 5-min of SWE, more glucose was co-extracted together with HG, RG-I and RG-II.

web.title: Ultrasound- and Microwave-Assisted Extraction of Pectin from Apple Pomace and Its Effect on the Quality of Fruit Bars
web.description:
Despite the fact that apple pomace is primarily used as animal feed or fertilizer, it is a substantial source of functional components such as carbohydrates, dietary fibers (including pectin), phenolic compounds, and others [2]. The pectin derived from apple pomace is used in the pharmaceutical, food, cosmetic, and other industries, where it serves as a biopolymer, preservative, antioxidant, anticorrosive agent, protective agent for diverse surfaces, etc. [2,3]. Fibers obtained from fruits offer an advantage over cereal fibers due to their superior solubility, lower phytic acid content, and the presence of bioactive molecules associated with antioxidant activity [4]. Pectin is industrially obtained from apple pomace through conventional extraction (CE) methods, such as using hot acidified water with either mineral acids (sulfuric, hydrochloric, nitric) or organic acids (citric, malic, oxalic) from pH 1.5 to 3.0 and temperatures ranging from 60 to 100 °C for 0.5 to 6 h, followed by alcoholic precipitation [2,5,6].

Several studies have confirmed that the antioxidant activity (AA) of pectin is influenced by the structure and composition of its chains, as well as by the presence of co-extracted contaminants in the polysaccharide matrix, which are associated with polyphenols, proteins, and other antioxidants [19,20,21,22]. Apple pectin, depending on its concentration, exhibited an approximately 5-fold greater DPPH radical-scavenging effect compared to other polysaccharides [23].
The pectin extraction method also influences AA. Pectin obtained by unconventional methods from various sources, with lower degree of esterification (DE) and higher anhydrogalacturonic acid (AUA) content, exhibits a higher AA compared to pectin extracted through CE [11,24,25]. Wang et al. [26] reported that pectic polysaccharides extracted with hot-compressed water from apple pomace showed in vitro AA and an inhibitory effect on free radicals. The IC~50~ values of such pectin oscillated between 1.4–3.5 mg/mL for 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) scavenging and about 1 mg/mL for 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS).

**The objective of this study** was to examine the impact of unconventional extraction methods, such as ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) and microwave-assisted extraction (MAE), on the yield, properties, and antioxidant activity of raw pectin extracted from apple pomace. The study also aimed to assess the potential of pectin as a binding and coating agent in the production of dried fruit bars; the protective effect of pectin films on functional products during storage was also investigated.

The following physicalchemical indicators of the apple pomace (AP) were determined: titratable acidity [48]; moisture and ash content [49]; fat content using Soxhlet extraction [50]; protein content [51]; total dietary fiber [52]; and insoluble dietary fiber [53]. The content of soluble substances was determined with a Kruss DR 201-95 digital refractometer (Kruss, Hamburg, Germany).

For the production of bars, a sample of pectin extracted through MAE for 10 min, at pH~2, in the ratio LSR 20 (__v/w__) was selected. According to the results, the MAE method ensures a higher yield (13.54%). The selected pectin had optimal characteristics required for a binding and coating agent. The aqueous solution of pectin (4.0%) with the addition of citric acid (0.04%) was prepared by dissolving the pectin in distilled water at 40 ± 1 °C with continuous stirring until complete dissolution.

First, 0.5 g of sample (AP powder or ground bars) was placed into a volumetric flask and made up to a volume of 50 mL with a 50% (__v/v__) aqueous solution of ethanol. The obtained samples were extracted using the ultrasound-assisted method (ISOLAB Laborgeräte GmbH, Eschau, Germany) at a frequency of 37 kHz and a temperature of 40 ± 1 °C, for a duration of 30 min. It was followed by centrifugation at 4000 rpm for 10 min, then separation and analysis of the supernatant (extract) [62].
### 2.8. Total Polyphenols and Flavonoids by Folin–Ciocâlteu
The total polyphenol content (TPC) and flavonoid content (TFC) were determined spectrophotometrically using well-known methods [63] with some modifications [62].
The TPC was determined using the Folin–Ciocâlteu phenol reagent [64] in relation to a calibration curve with gallic acid standard (0–500 mg/L, R^2^ = 0.9977) and expressed in milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per 1 g of dried sample weight (mg GAE/g DW).
The TFC was determined with AlCl~3~·6H~2~O according to the quercetin (0–160 mg/L, R^2^ = 0.9972) calibration curve. The results were expressed in milligrams of quercetin equivalents per 1 g of sample DW (mg QE/g DW).

Through the MAE method, pectin was extracted with a higher yield ranging from the minimum value of 1.18% (pH of 2.5, LSR of 10 (__v/w__), and 5 min extraction time) to the maximum value of 19.88% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), for 10 min), compared to the UAE pectin yield, with values between 0.98% (pH~2.5, LSR de 10 (__v/w__), for 15 min) and 9.91% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), for 30 min).

The MeO content in pectin extracted from __Golden Delicious__ apple pomace depends on the applied method of extraction. The results in Table 3 show that the MeO concentration declines with decreasing pH and increasing extraction time, while it is less reliant on LSR.
In MAE, pectin with a minimum MeO content of 4.88% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), for 10 min) was obtained and a maximum of 6.39% (pH~2.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), for 5 min). In UAE, the lowest MeO content was of 5.05% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), 30 min) and the highest was of 6.81% (pH~2.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), 15 min) (Table 3).

The purity of the extracted pectin is determined by the content of galacturonic acid, which should be higher than 65% [84]. The research results (Table 3) have shown that the AUA content in pectin obtained through UAE and MAE methods varies from sample to sample, depending on the extraction conditions, and increases with decreasing pH, increasing LSR, and longer extraction times, as shown in Table 3.
The UAE pectin had a higher purity compared to MAE. In the UAE method, the minimum AUA content was 49.16% (pH~2.5, LSR of 15 (__v/w__), for 15 min) and the maximum was 78.71% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), for 30 min). The MAE pectin had AUA content of a minimum of 47.31% (pH~2.5, LSR of 10 (__v/w__), 5 min) and a maximum of 73.02% (pH~1.5, LSR of 20 (__v/w__), 10 min).

web.title: Chemical and Bioactive Characterization of Spanish and Belgian Apple Pomace for Its Potential Use as a Novel Dermocosmetic Formulation
web.description:
The apple pomace that remains after juice extraction and cider production (circa ¼ of the fresh fruit weight) consists of leftover flesh, peels, seeds, and stems of different apple varieties [8,9]. Despite being naturally considered as waste, these residual materials are rich in bioactive compounds, particularly polyphenols, fibers, vitamins, and carotenoids [10]. Although some polyphenols are transferred to juice during the processing step, most remain in apple peel and, consequently, in apple pomace. Phytochemicals and active compounds present in the latter also include dietary fiber, pectin, triterpenoids, and volatile compounds. Pectin is known for its application as a gelling agent, being employed in different industrial sectors (food, pharmaceutics, and cosmetics), playing also several biological and physiological functions in human organisms. These functional properties make pectin a promising nutraceutical with low toxicity and production cost [11,12,13].

Thus, the present study intends to explore and describe the phenolic composition and bioactivity (antioxidant and antimicrobial) of apple pomace to validate its potential as an innovative source of cosmeceuticals to be included in new natural formulations, adding value to this material currently considered as industrial bio-waste. In addition to this main purpose, an additional preliminary characterization of its proximate composition was also performed to assess potential food applications. Moreover, instead of using typical commercial gelling agents (such as carbopol 940), we intended to isolate pectin from apple pomace by hot acid extraction, thus using this by-product considering two distinct aims.

2.6. Pectin Extraction Pectin was obtained by hot acid extraction, following a previously established procedure [24], with minor modifications. In brief, 50 g of frozen apple pomace was mixed with 200 mL of distilled water and heated to 90 °C under continuous stirring (350 rpm). Hydrochloric acid was added to decrease the pH to 1.5 or 3. The slurry was cooled using an ice bath for 30 min and the liquid portion was separated by centrifugation at 6000 rpm for 30 min at 15 °C. The supernatants were then vacuum filtered over a Buchner funnel with Whatman No. 4 filter paper. The remaining solids were centrifuged and filtered under the same conditions and the supernatants were combined, with a final pH readjustment to 3.5 with 1 M sodium hydroxide. The extract was then mixed with an equal volume of ethanol and stirred for 10 min at room temperature. The precipitate was separated by centrifugation under the same conditions mentioned above, dispersed in 500 mL of 70% ethanol, and stirred (10 min, 250 rpm, room temperature). The extracted pectin was freeze-dried (Labconco FreeZone 4.5, Kansas City, MO, USA) at −50 °C and 0.22 mbar for approximately 60 h. The yield was gravimetrically determined according to the following equation:% 𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑛 = 𝑚~𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑛/𝑚~𝑎𝑝𝑝~ × 100(5) where m~pectin~ is the mass of pectin obtained and m~app~ is the total mass of frozen apple pomace used in the extraction.

Phenolic Compounds In order to investigate the effect of the extraction step on phenolic compounds’ yield and bioactivity performance, four different extracts of each apple pomace sample were prepared by maceration, using the same solid:liquid ratio (1:30) with different solvents—namely water, ethanol, ethanol:water (80:20, v/v), and methanol:water (80:20, v/v)—and the results are presented in Table 2. Extraction yields with different solvents show statistically significant differences (p < 0.05) between samples, which might,

Regarding the apple pomace samples provided by the Spanish company (Table 3), fifteen different phenolic compounds were identified: three phenolic acids (peaks 1 to 3), four flavan-3-ols (peaks 4 to 7), five flavonoids (peaks 9–11, 13, and 14), and three di-hydrochalcones (peaks 8, 12, and 15).

In addition to their higher diversity, the extracts obtained from the Spanish apple pomace also presented the highest concentration of phenolic compounds, as was particularly obvious for EtOH (301 mg/100 g dw), MeOH:H~2~O (375 mg/100 g dw), and EtOH:H~2~O (197 mg/100 g dw) extracts.

Furthermore, the major compound found in the Spanish apple pomace extract was 5-O-caffeoylquinic acid, with concentrations between 66 and 114 mg/100 g dw for hydroethanolic and ethanolic extracts, respectively.

Among the three studied samples extracted with different solvents, the hydromethanolic and hydroethanolic extracts from the Spanish apple pomace samples showed the highest antioxidant activity with the lowest EC~50~ values in all assays except for the β-carotene bleaching inhibition, for which the ethanolic extract proved to be more effective. These results were somehow predictable given the phenolic profile presented by the Spanish apple pomace hydromethanolic extract, which presented the greatest amount of total phenolics compared to the other studied extracts.

Dermocosmetic Gel Formulation and Characterization In order to obtain a formulation free of artificial ingredients as much as possible, pectin extracted from the apple pomace samples was employed as a gelling agent. This methodology was conducted in our lab for the first time, being especially optimized for the current work. Thus, different pH conditions were assayed, allowing to achieve pectin extraction yields varying from 1.69 up to 1.87% to be further incorporated in the formulated hydrogel.

Conclusions Considering the main goal of the present study, it can be concluded that the selected drying method has a high influence over the phenolic profile, since the lyophilized samples presented a higher diversity and concentration of these compounds. Additionally, it was also verified that the chosen solvent has a considerable effect with different outcomes among thermally dried or freeze-dried samples; in fact, in the case of Spanish samples, methanol:water (375 mg/100 g dw) and ethanol (301 mg/100 g dw) led to the highest yields, while the corresponding result was obtained with water (132 mg/100 g dw) and the water:ethanol mixture (71 mg/100 g dw) in the case of Belgian samples. Taking the former results into account, and considering the lipid composition of human skin, the hydroethanolic extract was chosen to be added to the hydrogel as it is also much less toxic than methanol. Regarding the bioactivity of the extracts, the hydroethanolic extract presented good antibacterial activity against P. acnes (MIC = 2.5 mg/mL), MRSA (MIC = 2.5 mg/mL), and Proteus mirabilis (MIC = 10 mg/mL); the result obtained for P. acnes is especially important, as this bacterium is associated with skin disorders, such as acne. For the dermal hydrogel formulation, pectin was obtained by hot acid extraction; however, this method, at an industrial scale, produces pectin with a lower degree of polymerization and produces high amounts of chemical waste. Therefore, the study of possible alternative methods, such as enzymatic extraction, would be interesting for future research in this field. The resulting hydrogel was shown to have antioxidant and antimicrobial activity against P. acnes at a concentration of 5 mg/mL, thus validating its application as a cosmeceutical. web.title: Sustainable Exploitation of Apple By-Products: A Retrospective Analysis of Pilot-Scale Extraction Tests Using Hydrodynamic Cavitation
web.description:
To date, more than 60 phenolic compounds have been found in apples, namely phenolic acids (hydroxycinnamic and hydroxybenzoic acids), flavanols (catechin, epicatechin, procyanidin B2), flavonols (quercetin, isoquercetin), dihydrochalcones (phloretin and its glucoside phlorizin), and anthocyanins [2,3], differently distributed in peels, flesh, and seeds.

While most apple fruits are aimed at direct consumption, about 11.6 Mtons/year of fresh fruit are processed to obtain apple products, leading to about 3.5 Mtons/year of by-products also known as apple pomace (AP), which is usually discarded or used for animal feeding [7]. AP is composed of peels and flesh (95%), seeds (2–4%), and stem (1%), and its dietary fiber content consists of pectin, cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [8].
The proximate and analytical compositions of AP depend on the variety and origin of apples, as well as on the pre- or post-harvest interventions, such as pressing and other processes to obtain juice, cider, wine, and distilled spirits [9]. Based on published data, total sugars compose up to 50% of the dry matter, total dietary fiber around 27%, fat and protein up to 4% each, while the total phenolic content amounts to about 300 mg GAE/100 g [10]. Dominant phenolics in AP are similar to the whole fruit [11]. Due to the lower water content compared to the whole fruit and the higher content of phenolic compounds, AP represents an interesting low-cost source of phytochemicals and bioactive compounds [3,12].

Conventional extraction techniques of phenolic compounds from whole apples and AP include Soxhlet using ethanol as a solvent and maceration with pressurized hot water. Soxhlet extraction still represents the standard method for solid–liquid extraction and has shown efficacy in the isolation of compounds like phlorizin, epicatechin, quercetin, and phloretin from AP with a yield of phenolic compounds equal to 4.13 mg/g [29]. However, this method presents several drawbacks, including long process time, large solvent volumes and wastewater and toxic solid waste streams [30].

web.title: Effect of pectinase treatment on extraction of antioxidant phenols from pomace, for the production of puree-enriched cloudy apple juices
web.description:
In the case of apple juices, another factor of influence is the processing technology (Eberhardt, Lee, & Liu, 2000;Thielen, Will, Zacharias, Dietrich, & Jacob, 2004;Thielen et al., 2006;Watzl & Leitzmann, 1999). During apple processing into apple juice, the loss of 50-90% of the healthy polyphenols is unavoidable (Dietrich et al., 2003).

They have indicated that, in addition to the polyphenols, cloudy apple juice also contains cancer-preventive cloud particles. These particles are hydrocolloids with an architectural structure composed of a positively-charged nucleus of proteins, which is surrounded and complexed by negatively charged polysaccharides, such as pectins. As a whole, these colloids are encapsulated by a hydrate shell. Recent studies have shown that cell-wall polysaccharides develop secondary structures forming hydrophobic pockets for complex polyphenols during juice processing (Le Bourvellec, Bouchet, & Renard, 2005). Pectins are relatively stable throughout the gastric and small intestinal passage and are finally metabolised in the colon. Sembries, Dongowski, Mehrländer, Will, and Dietrich (2005) hypothesise that these cloud colloids might serve as vectors, transferring the entrapped polyphenols into the colon and might be responsible for the observed antiproliferative and health-promoting cancerpreventive bioactive effect of cloudy juice.

analysis Directly after juice pressing a portion of apple pomace (100 g) was frozen and freeze-dried (24 h; Christ Alpha 1-4 LSC, Martin Christ Gefriertrocknungsanlagen GmbH, Osterode am Harz, Germany). A homogeneous powder was obtained, by crushing the dried tissues with a closed laboratory mill to avoid hydration, and analysed. 2.5. Isolation of soluble and insoluble fractions Juice polysaccharides were isolated by alcoholic precipitation. Ten millilitres of juice were mixed with 50 mL of 96% ethanol. The mixture was thoroughly stirred for 5 min and stored for 24 h at 4 °C. After centrifugation (4200g for 10 min, at 4 °C), the supernatant was discarded, and the residue was dissolved in 10 mL of water (60 °C). Water-insoluble material was removed by centrifugation and freeze dried, weighed and obtained as an insoluble fraction. The supernatant was precipitated again with five volumes of ethanol. The residue obtained after centrifugation was freezedried, and finally weighed as a soluble fraction. Direct phloroglucinolysis of freeze-dried apple juice insoluble and soluble precipitates was performed as described below.

In the production of fruit juices, the degradation of pectin in the primary cell wall matrix and in the middle lamella is necessary to break the water binding capacity of pectin, which in turn allows maximal puree levels to be expelled and thus enhances the utilisation of the pulp (Le Bourvellec et al., 2005).

The composition and characterisation of polyphenolic compounds in fresh juices, apple pomace, and puree-enriched cloudy juices after enzymatic treatment is summarised in Table 2. The total content of phenolic compounds in apple pomace was higher than in raw juices (1520 mg/kg and 441 mg/L, respectively). Apple phenolics are mainly localised in the peel and in the seeds. Due to the low extraction yields during juice production, most of the phenolic compounds are retained in the pomace. Therefore, the content of phenolic compounds was higher in pomace than in raw juices. Analysis of apple pomace revealed a reasonably high content of polymeric procyanidins and flavan-3-ols, dihydrochalcones and flavonols. Polymeric procyanidins, dihydrochalcones and flavonols represented 57.0%, 5.5%, 3.0% and 24.0%, 2.6%, 0.5% of total polyphenols in pomace and fresh juices, respectively. Based on juice production, apple pomace is generated as the primary waste product. Consequently, in this study, we decided to apply a suitable enzyme treatment that would enable release or facilitate extraction of antioxidant phenols from apple pomace. During the enzymatic treatment, apple pomace was consistently liquefied, which caused an increase in the total phenolics content in mixed juices. In all juices mixed with pomace, especially after enzymatic treatment, a statistically significant increase in the content of phenolic compounds was observed, as compared to the fresh juices.

The total phenolic yields were higher in juice after treatment with Pectinex AFP L-4, Pectinex Yield Mash and Pectinex XXL, as compared to the untreated control (Table 2). These compound yields were not increased in pomace treated with Pectinex Ultra SPL (538 mg/L) and in the control sample (530 mg/L). The treatment of apple pomace with Pectinex AFP L-4, Yield Mash and XXL gave a statistically significant increase in contents of phloretin 2 0 -O-xyloglucose and phloretin 2 0 -O-glucose, flavonol glucosides and polymeric procyanidins in juices, compared to the fresh apple juices and control juices.

Recently, pectolytic and cellulolytic enzymes have been used for apple pomace liquefaction (Will, Bauckhage, & Dietrich, 2000). The juices produced contained significantly higher contents of polyphenolics, especially phloridzin, phloretin xyloglucoside and quercetin glycosides, than the control samples produced by mash maceration with pectolytic enzymes.

Phenolic compounds Most of the enzymatic preparations increased polymeric procyanidins contents in puree-enriched cloudy juices with the exception of Pectinex Ultra SPL and Pectinex Smash XXL. This was likely to be due to the specific influence of the enzyme on apple pomace. In the other juices obtained after enzymatic treatment of pomace, the concentration of polymeric procyanidins was observed to increase, which may indicate that both the cell-wall and vacuolar membrane had to be degraded enzymatically to enable optimal recovery of these compounds. This finding would be consistent with the localisation of procyanidins mainly in the cell wall and the fact that they can form bridges between readily soluble pectin and insoluble protopectin.
